title: The Story of Mexico's Dia de los Muertos
paragraphs: Orange flowers fill the streets, candles light up family altars and sugar skulls appear in shops — this is Mexico's Dia de los Muertos, or "Day of the Dead."

People often confuse this celebration with Halloween, but the Day of the Dead has its own unique traditions and history. It takes place over two days — typically November 1 and November 2 — and it's a time to honor deceased loved ones.
This holiday has roots in Indigenous traditions that may date as far back as the Olmec civilization over 3,000 years ago.

These early practices were passed down through later civilizations like the Maya and the Toltecs until they reached the Aztecs — who believed that, after death, the soul travels to an underworld called Mictlan. This journey could be long and difficult, and the dead needed help from their loved ones to reach Mictlan.
Families would leave offerings of food, water and personal belongings when a loved one died, to help guide the spirits and honor them.

In the 16th century, Spanish colonizers arrived in Mexico, bringing with them new religious traditions. In Catholicism, November 1 is All Saints' Day — a day to honor all the saints who have reached heaven — while November 2 is All Souls' Day, a day to remember and pray for people who have died.
Over time, elements of these different traditions came together, making Dia de los Muertos an important part of Mexican culture.
Every year in towns and cities across Mexico, the streets are decorated with flowers and skeletons, and people paint their faces to look like skulls.

Many families build ofrendas in their homes or by the graves of their loved ones. An ofrenda is a type of altar decorated with candles, flowers and photos of the deceased, as well as some of their favorite items and foods.

Families believe these offerings help welcome the spirits of their loved ones back for a visit, making Dia de los Muertos a celebration of life and the memories that keep people connected, even after death.
